sections.overview: Adelphobates quinquevittatus is a small poison frog of the southern Amazon, associated particularly with the Rio Madeira drainage in Brazil. Its contrasting orange, black and pale-striped pattern makes it conspicuous on the forest floor. Its reproduction is still poorly known, and recent field observations have added details about where its tadpoles develop.
sections.identification: The frog has a dark dorsal surface crossed by pale longitudinal stripes, an orange-toned body and dark markings on the limbs. A Brazilian field study identified individuals by this combination of orange coloration, black spots on all four legs and a black back with white stripes. In a measured sample of 14 frogs from Rondônia, snout–vent length was 15.9–18.9 mm (mean 17.71 mm) and head width 5.0–5.8 mm; the report does not separate these measurements by sex. Compare its pattern with other regional poison frogs, using locality and stripe arrangement as well as color. A reliable adult body-mass range was not found in the consulted species sources; the available field sample reports body length and head width, not mass.
sections.habitat: It inhabits humid tropical forest in the southern Amazon, including the Madeira drainage in the Brazilian states of Rondônia and Amazonas. Adults are reported in leaf litter and on fallen trunks on the forest floor. The documented range is centered on Brazil; older reports from neighboring countries are not uniformly confirmed by recent, photographically verified records.
sections.diet: The species eats small, abundant prey. A reproductive-ecology paper cites ants (Formicidae) and termites (Isoptera) among likely foods based on poison-frog diet studies. That prey list is broad rather than a quantified species-specific diet, and no seasonal measurements were found in the sources reviewed.
sections.behavior: The species is diurnal and uses leaf litter and fallen wood as shelter on the forest floor. Field observations found adults close to water-holding plant structures used by tadpoles. The available studies are limited in duration and place, so they do not establish a complete daily activity pattern or social system.
sections.reproduction: Eggs are laid terrestrially, and after hatching adults transport tadpoles to small water-filled plant structures. A field report documented tadpoles in the water-holding spadix of Attalea speciosa and in Brazil-nut fruit husks nearby; the authors suggested the larger spadix could hold more tadpoles, while dispersal among several sites may reduce losses from predation or cannibalism. These observations come from a limited study site, not a complete description of all breeding sites.
sections.ecology: Like other poison frogs, A. quinquevittatus contains defensive alkaloids; a species paper reports histrionicotoxins and pumiliotoxin-A. Its breeding depends on small water reservoirs in the forest, including palm inflorescences and fruit husks, linking frog reproduction to forest structure and the availability of phytotelmata. The exact ecological role and toxicity risk to humans are not quantified here.
sections.conservation: A current global IUCN category and a population trend were not verified in the sources used for this profile. A Brazilian field paper emphasizes that reproduction is insufficiently studied and notes the importance of preserving forest structures that hold water for tadpoles. The field observations point to a habitat requirement, not by themselves to a measured population decline.
